group.title: Character in depth
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Extremely generous, especially with money.
examples: A {munificent} donor paid for the new library wing.
wrong: The munificent patron refused to give a single coin.

words.meaning: Very unwilling to spend money; also, very poor.
examples: His {penurious} uncle reused the same tea bag for days.
wrong: The penurious host spent a fortune on gifts for everyone.

words.meaning: Very careful to follow rules, details and correct behavior.
examples: She is {punctilious} about replying to every letter within a day.
wrong: He was punctilious, so he ignored the rules and missed every detail.

words.meaning: Showing great care and steady, hard work.
examples: Thanks to {assiduous} research, the book is full of rare facts.
wrong: His assiduous effort meant he barely tried at all.

words.meaning: Lazy and avoiding activity or effort.
examples: The {indolent} clerk let the paperwork pile up for months.
wrong: He was so indolent that he worked fourteen hours a day.

words.meaning: Weak, irresponsible and unable to get things done.
examples: Her {feckless} brother lost yet another job through laziness.
wrong: The feckless manager handled every crisis with steady skill.

words.meaning: Praising powerful people too much to gain an advantage.
examples: The director was surrounded by {sycophantic} assistants who agreed with everything.
wrong: His sycophantic remarks openly insulted the boss.

words.meaning: Too polite and flattering in a way that seems false.
examples: The salesman’s {unctuous} smile made us trust him even less.
wrong: His unctuous manner was blunt, plain and honest.

words.meaning: Behaving as if you are better than other people.
examples: The waiter gave our cheap wine a {supercilious} glance.
wrong: She was supercilious, treating everyone as her superior.

words.meaning: Proud and commanding, expecting to be obeyed.
examples: With an {imperious} wave, she sent the servants away.
wrong: His imperious manner made him ask meekly for permission.

words.meaning: Too proud of yourself and boastful about your achievements.
examples: The general’s {vainglorious} speeches irritated his own troops.
wrong: The vainglorious champion never once mentioned his wins.

words.meaning: Modest and not wanting to draw attention to yourself.
examples: The {self-effacing} scientist gave all the credit to her team.
wrong: Being self-effacing, he talked about his own genius all night.

words.meaning: Saying very little; not inclined to talk.
examples: The {taciturn} farmer answered our questions with a nod.
wrong: Her taciturn friend chatted nonstop for three hours.

words.meaning: Very talkative.
examples: Our {loquacious} guide filled every silence with stories.
wrong: The loquacious man barely said a word all evening.

words.meaning: Friendly and enjoying company, food and drink.
examples: The dinner was {convivial}, full of laughter and good wine.
wrong: The convivial host avoided guests and ate alone.

words.meaning: Easily made angry.
examples: The {irascible} editor shouted at anyone who missed a deadline.
wrong: He was irascible, never once losing his temper.

words.meaning: Bad-tempered and ready to argue or complain.
examples: A {cantankerous} neighbor complained about every party on the street.
wrong: The cantankerous old man agreed pleasantly with everyone.

words.meaning: Quick to argue or fight; aggressively defiant.
examples: The {truculent} player argued with the referee after every call.
wrong: He grew truculent and meekly accepted every ruling.

words.meaning: Eager to argue, quarrel or fight.
examples: The {pugnacious} senator relished every heated debate.
wrong: Her pugnacious nature made her avoid all conflict.

words.meaning: Refusing stubbornly to change your mind.
examples: Despite every appeal, the landlord remained {obdurate}.
wrong: She was obdurate and changed her mind at the first request.

words.meaning: The courage and strength of character to face difficulty.
examples: The storm tested the young captain’s {mettle}.
wrong: He showed his mettle by running away at the first sign of trouble.

words.meaning: Calm and not easily excited or upset.
examples: The {phlegmatic} pilot calmly announced the engine failure.
wrong: Being phlegmatic, she panicked at the smallest problem.

words.meaning: Staying calm whatever happens.
examples: The {imperturbable} butler served dinner as the ceiling leaked.
wrong: The imperturbable nurse screamed when the alarm went off.

words.meaning: Honest and innocent, with no wish to trick anyone.
examples: The child’s {guileless} questions embarrassed the adults.
wrong: The guileless swindler planned every trick with care.

words.meaning: Innocent, trusting and open, sometimes too much.
examples: It was {ingenuous} of him to believe every promise the seller made.
wrong: She was ingenuous, suspicious of everyone and everything.

words.meaning: Deceitful; saying one thing while doing another.
examples: The {duplicitous} agent was working for both sides.
wrong: Her duplicitous nature meant she was always perfectly honest.

words.meaning: Not telling the truth; lying.
examples: The report was a {mendacious} account designed to hide the losses.
wrong: His mendacious statement was completely accurate and true.

words.meaning: Willing to betray people who trust you.
examples: The {perfidious} ally switched sides in the middle of the war.
wrong: His perfidious friend stood loyally by him for life.

words.meaning: Willing to act dishonestly in return for money.
examples: The {venal} official signed any permit for a bribe.
wrong: The venal judge refused every bribe he was offered.

words.meaning: Complete honesty and strong moral principles.
examples: Her {probity} made her the obvious choice to manage the fund.
wrong: His probity was clear from the money he stole.

words.meaning: Morally correct behavior and thinking.
examples: The judge was admired for his {rectitude} and fairness.
wrong: Her rectitude led her to cheat whenever she could.

words.meaning: Greedy and taking everything you can, often by force.
examples: {Rapacious} developers bought up the coastline.
wrong: The rapacious landlord lowered the rent out of kindness.

words.meaning: Spending money or resources in a reckless, wasteful way.
examples: His {profligate} spending left the company deep in debt.
wrong: Being profligate, she saved every spare penny.

words.meaning: Not allowing yourself much food, drink or pleasure.
examples: An {abstemious} man, he drank only water at the feast.
wrong: The abstemious guest ate and drank everything in sight.

words.meaning: Acting as if you are morally better than others.
examples: His {sanctimonious} lectures about honesty annoyed the whole office.
wrong: She was sanctimonious, never judging anyone’s behavior.

words.meaning: Lacking courage; timid and cowardly.
examples: The {pusillanimous} council backed down at the first protest.
wrong: The pusillanimous knight charged the dragon alone.

words.meaning: Brave and not afraid of danger.
examples: The {intrepid} explorers crossed the frozen sea on foot.
wrong: The intrepid traveler refused to leave her hotel room.

words.meaning: Rude and lacking respect, especially toward older people.
examples: The {impudent} student mocked the teacher’s accent.
wrong: His impudent reply was polite and deeply respectful.

words.meaning: Polished, elegant and confident in social situations.
examples: The {urbane} diplomat charmed every guest at the embassy.
wrong: The urbane host was clumsy, rude and awkward.

words.meaning: Rude and mean-spirited in a way that seems ungracious.
examples: It would be {churlish} to refuse such a generous offer.
wrong: Thanking them warmly was a churlish thing to do.
